title: Thailand’s MPC held at 1% as stronger technology exports did little for household demand
summary: All six members present at the Bank of Thailand’s 22 and 28 October meeting voted to keep the policy rate at 1.00%. The minutes, published on 11 November, explain why better-than-expected export and investment momentum did not call for a tighter stance. Growth was concentrated in activities with relatively little domestic labour or value added. Meanwhile, headline inflation was expected to rise temporarily, partly because of energy and weather, while weak domestic demand restrained underlying prices. The committee judged accommodative policy appropriate alongside targeted support for vulnerable borrowers, and identified longer-term financial risks from maintaining low rates (pp. 1–4).

Electronics and computer-parts exports helped improve the trade balance despite more expensive energy imports. The committee projected a balanced current account in 2026 and a surplus in 2027. But the technology cycle provided less support for household income than gross export figures might suggest. AI-related exports had an import content of 68% among the largest 1% of exporters in the first eight months of 2026. That figure applies to a particular group of exporters and period. Data-centre investment was relatively light on labour. Meanwhile, debt, a fragile labour market and the cost of essentials constrained consumption, particularly for low-income households. The committee revised consumption down despite fiscal stimulus. Its growth projections were 2.4% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027 (p. 1).

The interpretation of activity data was itself changing. Expanded coverage of factories and products made the manufacturing index more representative of export activity. Staff used the revised series to assess quarterly momentum but said the year-on-year comparison depended on the forthcoming revision to historical national accounts. Tourism illustrated a different measurement problem. The projected number of visitors fell to 32.0 million in 2026 and 34.5 million in 2027 as higher travel costs affected short-haul arrivals. Expected receipts held up because visitors stayed longer and spent more on food and accommodation. Stable receipts alone would conceal the weaker flow of travellers (pp. 1–2).

Energy subsidies lowered the inflation forecast despite higher world oil prices. Headline inflation was expected to average 2.1% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027; the corresponding core projections were 1.2% and 1.3%. Higher fuel costs and El Niño could lift near-term prices, then weak demand and base effects would reduce the annual rate. This assessment rested partly on the Oil Fuel Fund’s ability to cushion domestic prices, which its financing constraints could impair. Stronger business pass-through could also lift core inflation. Medium-term expectations remained within target at the time of the meeting (p. 2).

Financing conditions varied sharply by borrower. Large corporates borrowed more for both higher operating costs and new projects, while SME lending contracted across most sectors. Private loan rates remained broadly stable even as government yields edged up and the baht weakened against the dollar. The committee linked the currency move to changing expectations for US policy and dearer oil, citing Thailand’s energy-import dependence. Reserves near US$280 billion, around 2.5 times short-term external debt, and relatively low foreign holdings of domestic assets offered some protection. Members still saw risks to corporate bond funding costs and to vulnerable borrowers’ ability to service debt (pp. 2–3).

Members saw no significant current buildup of financial instability. Their concern was that prolonged low rates could encourage leverage, risk-taking by savers and investment in projects with low productivity. They also flagged the risk of volatile currency and capital flows if confidence changed as major central banks tightened. This was a prospective risk assessment, without evidence of a particular risk premium being mispriced. Structural productivity problems and weak firms’ access to funding called for fiscal, financial and targeted measures alongside the policy rate (pp. 3–4).

questions.question: How much domestic income does the export recovery generate outside the leading firms?
questions.detail: The minutes give an import-content figure for a selected group and identify few jobs created by data centres. They do not establish the domestic value added of the entire expansion. For the growth and rates outlook, compare customs volumes and imported inputs with domestic supplier orders, payrolls and regional consumption. Revised official production and national-accounts data would help test whether the committee’s concern about limited spillovers is borne out.

questions.question: When could the Oil Fuel Fund stop shielding domestic prices?
questions.detail: Subsidies lower the baseline forecast, but the minutes identify financial constraints without publishing the size of the remaining cushion. For inflation-linked and baht exposures, inspect official fund accounts, financing arrangements and retail fuel-price rules under several oil-price paths. Compare the implied change in regulated consumer prices with subsequent prices in transport-intensive sectors to separate the immediate fuel effect from broad pass-through.

questions.question: Is the contraction in SME lending a shortage of working capital or a deterioration in borrower quality?
questions.detail: The committee describes cautious lenders and limited access while reporting stable aggregate credit quality. Different explanations imply different risks for Thai bank and corporate credit. Compare applications, approvals, pricing and subsequent arrears across borrowers with similar turnover and collateral. Supervisory lending surveys, bank disclosures and information from targeted financing programmes could show whether viable firms were being rationed or credit demand was falling alongside activity.
